notes: \cpara{Recaps ``Correspondence Bias,'' posted the day before, in three sentences.}

\cpara{Makes the post's first claim: the bias grows stronger when the act offends us. It rests on the author's observation (``I observe''); no study is cited. The advice follows: as a matter of prior probability, ask what the Enemy believes about the situation.}
\cpara{Introduces the example. The facts given are correct: nineteen hijackers, four airliners. A rhetorical question then states the view the post will reject.}

\clogic{No one is quoted holding this view. President Bush gave the ``hate freedom'' account to Congress on 20 September 2001 (see the note on ``Belief as Attire''), and explained the hatred by beliefs: the terrorists ``practice a fringe form of Islamic extremism'' and ``want to overthrow existing governments in many Muslim countries.'' The speech said nothing about how they were born.}
\cpara{States the central claim: everyone is the hero of their own story, so a portrait that makes the Enemy look bad will be wrong about what goes on in the Enemy's mind.}

\cfact{The post gives no evidence here. There is some for ordinary conflicts. In autobiographical accounts collected by Baumeister, Stillwell and Wotman (1990), perpetrators portrayed their provoking behaviour ``as meaningful and comprehensible,'' while victims depicted it ``as arbitrary, gratuitous, or incomprehensible.'' The study concerns everyday quarrels, not political violence.}

\cpara{Explains why the distorted portrait persists: arguments are soldiers, so any factual correction reads as treason. The mechanism is the one in ``Politics is the Mind-Killer'' and ``Policy Debates Should Not Appear One-Sided,'' again given without evidence (see the notes there).}
\cpara{A two-sentence argument from frequency: monstrous acts are common in history, and rare dispositions cannot explain common acts.}
\cpara{Suggests, with ``maybe,'' another reason to prefer evil enemies: understanding might lead to forgiveness, and it is harder to kill people who are not ``pure darkness.''}

\cpara{Links the point to ``Policy Debates Should Not Appear One-Sided'': wanting an evil enemy is wanting a policy with no downside. In self-defence both options are tragedies, and the author prefers that the one who started the violence die.}
\cpara{Separates understanding from approval: an accurate picture of the Enemy's motives does not make the Enemy's beliefs true or the acts justified.}
\cpara{Offers a sign of an accurate picture: it will make you sad, not righteous. Horror is reserved for rarer cases.}

\clogic{Two religious groups are named, without evidence, as people whose beliefs have ``utterly destroyed their sanity.'' The post blames beliefs, not birth, so it keeps to the letter of its rule. It sits uneasily with the post's warning that construing motives which make the Enemy look bad will leave you ``flat wrong.''}

\cpara{Applies the argument to the hijackers: not evil mutants, not haters of freedom, but heroes of their own story, who in another environment might have been police officers. Three sentences keep understanding apart from approval.}

\cfact{As in ``Belief as Attire,'' which makes the same claim (see the note there), the post cites nothing the hijackers or their leaders said. Evidence that fits the claim was available. In a speech whose transcript Al Jazeera published on 1 November 2004, Osama bin Laden, who was not one of the nineteen, said that ``free men do not forfeit their security, contrary to Bush's claim that we hate freedom. If so, then let him explain to us why we don't strike for example -- Sweden?'' The speech named as the motive what it called the ``oppression and tyranny of the American/Israeli coalition'' in Palestine and Lebanon.}
